candidates.title: This Black Friday, Hisense wants your next TV to be a gaming screen, an art gallery, or both
candidates.full_text:
There was a time when Black Friday meant camping outside a Best Buy in a folding chair, all for a doorbuster TV that was roughly the size of a cereal box and twice as blurry. Those days are mostly gone, thankfully, along with the elbow jabs from angry shoppers. What hasn’t changed is the hunger: the TV is still the headline purchase of the season, the one big thing the whole household agrees on. What has changed is what that money buys. Tech that used to live exclusively in flagship sets now shows up in TVs that cost less than a decent couch, and Hisense is a big reason why.

Hisense’s current lineup reads like a Black Friday menu with four courses. The E7SF is the appetizer that punches above its weight, bringing MiniLED backlighting and a native 144Hz panel to sizes from 50 to 100 inches. Course two, the U6SF Pro, is made for bright rooms, with 1,200 nits, a glare-free screen, and a built-in subwoofer. The U7SG is the main course, packing up to 3,000 dimming zones, a 165Hz panel, and Google TV with Gemini on screens as big as 116 inches. Dessert is the CanvasTV, which hangs on your wall like framed art and shows off over 1,000 free artworks when you’re done watching. Pick a course, or pick two.

Somewhere in your house, there’s a TV that has been “good enough” for about seven years, and it has been lying to you about what black looks like the whole time. The E7SF calls that bluff at Hisense’s entry tier, with Hi-QLED MiniLED backlighting, up to 260 local dimming zones, and up to 600 nits of peak brightness, depending on size. A native 144Hz panel is there for fast plays and car chases, while AI Sports Mode is designed to spot a game on screen and tune the picture and crowd noise to match. AI Picture automatically adjusts brightness and color to suit the room, great news for anyone who never opens a settings menu. Movie purists get Filmmaker Mode, plus Dolby Vision IQ and HDR10+ Adaptive.

Gamers get AMD FreeSync Premium, Dolby Vision Gaming, and two HDMI 2.1 ports supporting 4K at 144Hz, plenty for current consoles. Fire TV with Alexa+ handles the software, so finding something to watch can be as simple as asking for it. The 50 through 85-inch models use a 2.0 speaker setup, while the 100-inch steps up to a 2.1 system with 50W of output. That 100-inch option is the real party trick here, putting a screen the size of a small wall at the entry point of Hisense’s MiniLED lineup. Black Friday discounts across the E7SF range go up to 52%.

Every sunny Sunday, there’s a moment around kickoff when the TV turns into a mirror and you end up watching your own silhouette sit on the couch. The U6SF Pro’s anti-reflection screen aims to spare you that view. Behind it sits a Hi-QLED MiniLED backlight with up to 600 local dimming zones and up to 1,200 nits of peak brightness, both varying by size. The aim is to keep a daytime game bright and saturated; the display also carries Pantone Validated color certification. A native 144Hz panel and AMD FreeSync Premium Pro support on most sizes cater to gaming, with two HDMI 2.1 ports for your consoles. The slim unibody design keeps the bezels thin.

Most TV speakers sound like they’re coming from inside a shoebox, but the U6SF Pro adds a built-in subwoofer to its 2.1 system, with Dolby Atmos and DTS Virtual:X support. That could give explosions some actual rumble and put off that soundbar purchase for another year. Fire TV with Alexa+ runs the show, so you press a button and ask for a program, a score, or the lights to dim. It also supports Wi-Fi 6 and carries IMAX Enhanced certification. Black Friday discounts go up to 52%, with sizes running up to 100 inches.

Not long ago, a 165Hz refresh rate was something you only found on gaming monitors parked two feet from your face. The U7SG puts it on a living room TV that goes up to 116 inches, which is a very different viewing distance. Behind that panel, up to 3,000 local dimming zones let it darken a shadowy corner independently of a stadium floodlight right next to it. Hisense rates peak brightness at up to 3,000 nits, with both figures varying by size. A dual-layer anti-glare treatment is designed to reduce reflections, and the display carries Pantone Validated color certification. candidates.title: 5 Knife and EDC Picks That Run From a Golden-Made Spyderco to a 650-Lumen Keychain Light
candidates.full_text:
Slip a slim BlackWash Leek against a taut cord and the 40% Amazon cut starts to feel secondary. The five Amazon picks below run from a Golden-made Spyderco Para Military 2 at $164.04 down to a 650-lumen keychain light at $23.76.

Every price was checked live on Amazon today. The spread covers a stocking stuffer, two daily carries under $75, and the Spyderco at the top of the list.

The Spyderco Para Military 2 rarely goes on sale, so the black G-10 build in CPM S45VN at $164.04 on Amazon is the news tonight. Nothing about the formula changed.

It’s still made in Golden, Colorado. The Compression Lock, four-position clip and 3.42-inch blade carry over unchanged.

Spyderco Para Military 2 3.42-inch CPM S45VN blade · Black G-10 handle · Compression Lock · Four-position pocket clip · Made in Golden, Colorado Price : $164.04 Where to buy : Amazon

The Kershaw Leek BlackWash has been the slim, USA-made answer to what you should actually carry for a long time, and Amazon has the 1660BLKW at $74.61 this weekend against a $124.99 list. A 3-inch Sandvik 14C28N blade and an assisted opener sit inside a stainless handle that disappears in a pocket. It’s the one to hand someone who wants a real brand folder without paying Benchmade or Spyderco money.

The Leek uses an assisted opener and a frame lock, not a crossbar. At 40% off, it’s the cheapest icon on tonight’s list by a wide margin.

Kershaw Leek BlackWash 3-inch Sandvik 14C28N blade · Assisted opening · Stainless BlackWash handle · Ken Onion design · Made in the USA Regular Price : $124.99 Deal Price : $74.61 You Save : $50.38 (40% off) Where to buy : Amazon

The Kizer Pokiman CD leads Kizer’s weekend cuts at $35.99 on Amazon, down $10 from its $45.99 list. The sale ends this weekend.

Its 3.16-inch D2 drop point opens boxes, cuts cord and slices an apple at lunch without any drama at all. The black G10 handle grips well wet or dry.

At 2.83 ounces it carries like a knife half its size, and the D2 edge holds up through a week of cardboard and strapping before it asks for a stone. Budget folders usually cut a corner you can feel in the first week. This one started in budget territory before the sale cut it further still.

Kizer Pokiman CD 3.16-inch D2 drop point blade · Black G10 handle · Clutch Lock · Pocket clip · 2.83 ounces Regular Price : $45.99 Deal Price : $35.99 You Save : $10.00 (22% off) Where to buy : Amazon

This Good Worker Damascus folder dropped to $32.40 on Amazon, half off its $64.90 list, and it’s a different animal from the karambit and the pink rescue knife we’ve covered from the brand before. The layered Damascus blade runs 2.95 inches, and the Guibourtia wood handle gives every knife its own grain, so no two look alike on a desk.

That’s gift-ready hardware at a stocking stuffer price. It’s why this knife got its own piece today instead of a line in somebody else’s sale story.

Most budget folders feel like gas station knives with better photos than steel, and this one doesn’t. It runs a ceramic ball bearing pivot, a liner lock and a deep carry clip.

Good Worker Damascus Folder 2.95-inch layered Damascus blade · Guibourtia wood handle · Ceramic ball bearing pivot · Liner lock · Deep carry clip Regular Price : $64.90 Deal Price : $32.40 You Save : $32.50 (50% off) Where to buy : Amazon

The RovyVon Aurora A5 closes the list at $23.76 on Amazon, against a $27.95 list. The fourth generation puts a 650-lumen front light, side lights and a glow-in-the-dark body into a light that lives on your keys, and it adds a metal button and USB-C charging. The side lights handle the close work, reading a fuse box or a keyhole without blasting the front beam.

The front emitter steps through 0.5, 25, 200 and 650 lumens on the high output build. Its rated throw reaches 110 meters at the top step.

Either build charges from the same cable that feeds your phone. A dead light at a campsite is a ten-minute top-up, not a ruined night.

candidates.title: FotorGear’s $209 Retro Camera brings back the waist-level viewfinder with a 13MP Sony sensor
candidates.full_text:
For years, FotorGear’s whole business was convincing your iPhone it was a camera. The Hong Kong brand built clip-on lenses, grips, and a retro photography kit that won Gold for Product Design at the 2024 London Design Awards, all to make a phone feel like something with a film door. With the Campix, the company finally stopped pretending and built the actual camera. It’s a 4.6-ounce (129g) digital shooter with a flip-up waist-level viewfinder, zero screens on the back, and a wind dial you turn between frames. Call it the logical endpoint of a company that kept bolting camera bits onto phones until the phone part became optional.

The design leans hard on the 1950s, especially the Exakta Varex, an East German SLR famous for letting you swap its prism for a waist-level hood. Campix shoots 36-frame digital rolls through a 13MP Sony sensor and a 26mm f/2.2 lens, with a recipe dial holding six film looks and a TTL xenon flash for nights out. The front T-mount takes the very same fisheye, wide, portrait, macro, and anamorphic lenses FotorGear sells for phones, so anyone with a drawer full of them just found those lenses a second home. Retail sits at $209, about a quarter of the $849 Fujifilm X half.

Flip open the lid on the Campix’s top plate and you find a small display recessed inside a hood, angled so you look straight down at it. That screen is your only window into the camera, showing battery level, the active film look, and how many frames remain on the roll. There’s no rear LCD and no playback, so every shot stays a mystery until it lands in the app. I’ve always loved how waist-level cameras change the body language of photography. You end up bowing toward the scene instead of aiming at it, and people tend to stay themselves when no lens is pointed at their face from eye height.

Every frame follows a little ritual: compose, press the red shutter button, then turn the thumb dial before the camera lets you fire again. FotorGear’s own diagram labels it a rewind dial, though in practice it behaves like a film winder. A second mechanical dial clicks between six film recipe slots, and each 36-frame roll commits you to one look, the same way loading Portra or Tri-X used to. Fujifilm offers a similar Film Camera Mode on the X half, but there it’s a setting you switch on, with the rear screen disabled and an optical tunnel finder taking over. Campix builds the entire camera around the constraint, and I find that a far more honest piece of design.

The imaging hardware is a Sony IMX258, a 13MP chip (4128 x 3096 pixels) at the 1/3.06-inch size you’d usually find inside a mid-range smartphone. Ahead of it sits a 26mm-equivalent f/2.2 lens built from four glass elements and two plastic ones, with fixed focus from about 3 feet (0.9m) to infinity. Exposure is fully automatic, ISO runs from 100 to 3200, and white balance can stay on auto or be set manually. That small sensor explains the tiny body and the price, and the files will land closer to good phone shots than to the X half’s 1-inch output. Fixed focus suits the waist-level style, which has always been about zone focusing and anticipating the moment.

The flash is a xenon tube with TTL metering, meaning it reads light through the lens to set its output, and it works best between roughly 3 and 10 feet (1 to 3m). Xenon throws a shorter, brighter burst than a phone’s LED, freezing motion with the crisp, slightly harsh look people chase on old Yashica T4s and Olympus Mju IIs. The 1000mAh battery is rated for about 400 shots with flash or 600 without, roughly 11 to 16 full rolls per charge. Files travel over Wi-Fi to the iOS and Android app or over USB-C, and the included lanyard doubles as a USB-C cable. The polycarbonate and metal body measures 3.8 x 1.4 x 2.3 inches (97 x 35 x 58mm), dressed in titanium-toned metal and leather.

The front of the Campix carries FotorGear’s T-mount, the same lens mount the company uses on its Retro series phone lenses. That lineup covers an 8mm fisheye, a 16mm wide-angle, a 60mm portrait lens, a 75mm macro, and a 1.55x anamorphic, and FotorGear confirms lenses already bought for a phone fit Campix directly. The stock lens also has a 37mm thread, so standard screw-on filters work, and the top bundle includes a star filter, a circular polarizer, and a UV filter.
